newsitem.title: CHINA: China bans novel that mirrors true-life scandal.
newsitem.headline: China bans novel that mirrors true-life scandal.

text.p: Chinese propaganda officials have banned a novel with a plot striking similar to a corruption scandal that led to the downfall of the most senior official of communist rule, Chinese sources said on Sunday.

The Propaganda Department of the Communist Party, the Ministry of Culture and the Press and Publications Administration issued a joint circular this month banning the sale of the novel "Wrath of Heaven", the sources said.
"The novel was banned because it's about real people and real events," one source, a government official, told Reuters.
It recounts the tale of a graft-buster who runs into huge difficulties while investigating a corruption scandal after the mysterious death of a vice-mayor.

The plot bears a striking resemblance to the disgrace of Chen Xitong, who resigned as Beijing's Communist Party boss in April 1995 after his protege, Vice-Mayor Wang Baosen, committed suicide after coming under investigation for corruption.
Chen was ousted from the Communist Party's powerful Politburo in September 1995, becoming the most senior official to be ensnared in a corruption scandal since the communists swept to power in 1949.

Chen has not been seen in public for two years. Hong Kong's China-watching newspapers say Chen is under house arrest in Inner Mongolia after losing out in a power struggle to China's Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin.
One of Chen's sons has been detained and his mistress remains on the run.
The novel may not be purely fiction.
"It was banned because it leaks major secrets," a second source said.
"Prosecutors suspect the author is one of the investigators because the novel reveals details previously unknown to outsiders."
The novel's author is Fang Wen, a pseudonym that is homonymous in Chinese with "just heard".

The author received 160,000 yuan ($19,000) for the book, the sources said. A publishing house in Inner Mongolia printed 5,000 copies, but many pirated copies have found their way on to the shelves of small bookshops in Beijing.
Propaganda officials and the publishing house could not be reached for comment.
Despite the ban, one small bookshop in the capital said the novel was in hot demand.
"One day I sold seven copies in just one hour," the bookshop owner said as he took out a copy from a hidden shelf after initially denying he had copies for sale.
The novel is a bombshell, the Chinese sources said.
"It must be banned... It only kindles the dissatisfaction of the masses with the current leadership," the government official said. "It is also affecting the morale of officials.
"The threat and the danger posed by such a novel to the current leadership is much bigger than pornographic publications," the official said.

Last week, the Communist Party's Discipline Inspection Commission issued the most detailed regulations in nearly a decade to tighten discipline, hinting at subversion within its own ranks as well as corruption and womanising.
Corruption, virtually unknown in China under the strict Stalinist rule of late party chairman Mao Zedong, has made a rapid comeback in nearly two decades of market reform.
